title: A streak is a tool, not a judge
description: A run of good days can motivate you, but a broken streak is information, not a verdict on your character.

body.heading: Why streaks work — and why they bite
paragraphs: Counting consecutive days is satisfying because each day adds a little weight to the next. Nobody wants to be the one who breaks a forty-day run. Used lightly, that pressure is genuinely helpful.

The trouble starts when the streak becomes the point. One missed day can feel like the whole thing is ruined, and people often abandon a good habit entirely over a single gap that, in the long run, matters very little.

body.heading: Soften the rules before you need to
paragraphs: Decide in advance what counts as a kept day, and make the smallest version count. Two minutes of practice on a chaotic day still counts. A short walk still counts. The habit survives because the bar bends instead of snapping.

You can also build in planned rest. Many people find “never miss twice” kinder and more durable than “never miss.” A miss is an accident; two in a row is the start of a new pattern, so the second day is where gentle effort pays off most.

body.heading: Count something kinder
paragraphs: If streaks make you anxious, count totals instead: practices this month, pages this week, walks since spring. Totals only ever go up, and they describe your real life more honestly than an unbroken chain.
However you count, remember what the number is for. It exists to encourage the habit. The moment it starts punishing you instead, change the counting, not the habit.

takeaway: Let the streak serve the habit — never the other way round.
